newsitem.title: USA: U.S., Japanese business leaders urge Japan reforms.
newsitem.headline: U.S., Japanese business leaders urge Japan reforms.

text.p: U.S. and Japanese business leaders on Wednesday urged Japan to speed up deregulation of its economy and called for steps to reduce swings in the yen-dollar exchange rate.

"A stable exchange rate that reflects the economic fundamentals of both countries is indispensable for the proper conduct of business," the business leaders said in a joint statement at the end of the 34th annual U.S.-Japan business conference here.
But they did not say how a stable exchange rate would be achieved, and some business leaders admitted that the rate would be set by the market.
The final statement reflected American anxiety that a recent weakening of the yen has boosted Japanese exports, leading to a sharp rise in Japan's trade surplus.

Ford Motor Co. Vice Chairman Wayne Booker voiced concern at the meeting on Tuesday that Japanese auto exports to the United States had risen this year, partly because of the weaker yen, whereas Ford sales in Japan had fallen.

More than 70 U.S. and Japanese business leaders, including a number of heads of multinational companies, discussed deregulation and market access, exchange rates and the role of the United States and Japan in Asia during the two-day meeting of the U.S.-Japan and Japan-U.S. business councils.

Both sides said the meeting, most of which was held behind closed doors, was very cooperative. "We had a great meeting. We feel very pleased about the progress made," said Michael Jordan, chairman of Westinghouse Electric Corp.

Toru Hashimoto, chairman of Fuji Bank Ltd., said the mood was much better than at similar meetings three years ago. He felt this was because "the American side has regained confidence" because of the buoyant U.S. economy.

In their final statement, the business leaders said "efforts to improve economic fundamentals" must continue in order to lessen the rise in the Japanese trade surplus and stabilize the yen/dollar exchange rate "within an appropriate range reflecting basic fundamentals."

The business leaders said, however, they had not agreed on a target for the exchange rate. The yen is currently trading at just under 113 to the dollar. Some U.S. manufacturers would like to see a slightly weaker dollar to bolster their exports to Japan.

The final statement said Japan must speed up deregulation "in its own interest to sustain economic growth." "Successful deregulation should result in increased market access and competition for foreign and domestic firms," the statement said, adding that market access remained a top priority for the business leaders.

American companies have long complained about restrictions on their access to the Japanese market. Both American and Japanese executives at the conference said deregulation would boost the Japanese economy, which has only just recovered from five years of near-recession.
The U.S. and Japanese business leaders also called for "free, fair, and global" world markets in information technology products and services.
They said they would form a joint task force to "evaluate the justification for future (environmental) standards" in preparation for a world conference on climate change in Kyoto, Japan, in December.

The final communique said the executives should explore how U.S. and Japanese businesses could contribute to economic growth in Asia by bringing together products, skills and financing in large infrastructure projects and how they could encourage investment and trade liberalization in the region.
